sections.name: Application
sections.description: Identity, environment class and the target this file belongs to.

sections.name: Database
sections.description:
Credentials for the role and database the registry declares for this
target. install-target-database reads them from here and never writes them.

sections.name: Cache / Redis
sections.description:
One Redis server per host, separated per target by REDIS_PREFIX and the
database numbers below.

sections.name: Queue
sections.description:
The queue connection and the Redis settings that back it. The queue NAME
is a registry property; what is configured here is how to reach it.

sections.name: Filesystem / Media
sections.description:
Where uploaded media is written and which disk serves it publicly, and the
lifecycle the stored originals and derived variants follow.

The lock settings are not tuning knobs to leave blank: variant generation and
the purge each take a lock so two workers cannot derive or delete the same
object at once, and a blank TTL is not a longer lock — it is an unreadable one.
Every value here is the current contract rather than a suggestion.

sections.name: Upload policy
sections.description:
The limits an upload is accepted or refused by, and the quality derived
variants are written at.

These are deliberately explicit rather than left to the application's defaults:
they are the operational policy of a brand — how large an image a visitor may
send, and how much the server will spend re-encoding it — and the values below
ARE those defaults, so making them visible changes nothing.

MAX_PIXELS guards total area independently of the width and height limits: a
6000x6000 image passes both and is still 36 megapixels to decode.

sections.name: Content lifecycle
sections.description:
How long content outlives the account, or the decision, that removed it.

A retention of 0 would delete immediately, and a blank one is not "forever" —
it is whatever the application's own default happens to be, which is the thing
a deployed target should not be left guessing at. The moderation retention is
deliberately blank: it is the one value here that is a policy decision per
brand rather than a platform default.

sections.name: Feed
sections.description:
How many posts a feed page serves, and the ceiling a caller may ask for.

FeedQuery reads both directly, so these are deployed performance policy: the
default decides the size of every feed query, and the maximum is what stops a
caller asking for the whole table. The values below are the application's own
defaults, made visible rather than changed.

sections.name: Import
sections.description:
Whether a visitor may create a post from an external URL. Off by default, and
off is a decision rather than an oversight: the importer fetches a
caller-supplied address from the server, so enabling it widens what the host
will connect to.

sections.name: Rate limits
sections.description:
Attempts per decay window, per action. The values below are the application's
current defaults, made explicit because they are abuse policy and belong where
an operator can see them — not because they are being changed.

sections.name: Sessions
sections.description:
SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE stays true everywhere: every deployed target is
served over HTTPS.

sections.name: Logging
sections.description:
Channel, stack and verbosity. Nothing here enables a remote sink; see
Sentry and Nightwatch below.

sections.name: Social login
sections.description:
Per-provider OAuth credentials. A provider is offered only when its own
switch is enabled AND both of its keys are present.

sections.name: Mail
sections.description:
Transport only. Which addresses are allowed to receive mail is an
application concern, not an environment one.

sections.name: Sentry
sections.description:
One Sentry project serves every target; SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT carries the
environment class and the target is distinguished by its own tag.

sections.name: Nightwatch
sections.description:
Disabled by default. The vendor default is enabled=true, so the key must
be present and explicit rather than omitted.

config_env_readers.$schema_note: config/*.php must name every environment variable it reads as a literal, so the inventory can see it. Two files legitimately read env() through a local closure that normalizes a blank value to unset; the KEY is still a literal at every call site, but the env() call itself is not. Those closures are declared here by name, so a NEW dynamic env() anywhere else fails the guard instead of quietly escaping the inventory.

read_outside_config.$schema_note: Laravel's rule is that env() is read in config/ only, and these are the exceptions the audit found. They are not part of a deployed target's .env contract because none of them is read while serving a request: each is an input to a command somebody runs deliberately. Recorded anyway so there is no third, silent category — a new env() read outside config/ fails the guard until it is accounted for here.
read_outside_config.ADMIN_PASSWORD: one-shot input to the create-admin-user command, supplied for that invocation and never stored in .env
read_outside_config.DEMO_ADMIN_PASSWORD: demo seeder only; never run on a deployed target
read_outside_config.DEMO_MODERATOR_PASSWORD: demo seeder only; never run on a deployed target

inventory_scope_note: The inventory scans this application's own config/*.php. A key read only by a config file Laravel ships inside the framework — one this application has not published — is outside that scope and therefore invisible to the guard. Two such keys are in the target contract today: BCRYPT_ROUNDS (vendor/laravel/framework/config/hashing.php) and BROADCAST_CONNECTION (.../config/broadcasting.php). They are genuinely read at runtime, so they belong in the templates; they simply cannot be derived by scanning config/. Widening the scan to the framework's own configs would inventory every Laravel default in existence, which is the opposite of the judgement this policy records. Publishing either config file would bring its keys into scope automatically.
